points: Nasutoceratops is a genus of ceratopsid dinosaur.
Nasutoceratops lived in North America.
Nasutoceratops lived during the Late Cretaceous.
Nasutoceratops lived about 76.0–75.5 million years ago.
The first known Nasutoceratops fossils were found in the Kaiparowits Formation at Grand Staircase–Escalante National Monument in southern Utah.
The first known Nasutoceratops specimens were discovered from 2006 onward.
The first finds comprised a subadult specimen and two other partial skull specimens.
The subadult specimen included a partial skeleton behind the skull.
The subadult specimen preserved rare skin impressions.
The subadult became the holotype of the newly named genus and species Nasutoceratops titusi in 2013.
The genus name Nasutoceratops means 'large-nosed horned face.'
The species name titusi honors paleontologist Alan L. Titus for his work recovering fossils at Grand Staircase–Escalante National Monument.
News reports drew attention to the dinosaur's large nose.
Nasutoceratops appeared in Jurassic World films.
The holotype skull is about 1.5 m (4.9 ft) long.
Nasutoceratops is estimated to have been 4.5 m (14.8 ft) long.
Nasutoceratops is estimated to have weighed 1.5 metric tons (1.7 short tons).
The snout of Nasutoceratops was unusually deep from top to bottom.
The snout of Nasutoceratops was unusually short from front to back.
The external nostril occupied 75% of the skull length in front of the eye sockets.
The nasal bones of Nasutoceratops may have contained air-filled spaces.
Air-filled nasal bones are unknown in other ceratopsians.
The nasal horn was low.
The nasal horn was blade-shaped.
The brow horns projected forward.
The brow horns spanned about 40% of the total skull length.
The bony cores of the holotype's brow horns reached 457 mm (18.0 in).
Nasutoceratops had the longest known brow horns of any centrosaurine, both absolutely and relative to skull size.
The brow horns have been compared to those of a Texas Longhorn bull.
The neck frill was nearly circular.
The neck frill was widest around the middle.
The accessory bones along the frill margin were shaped like low crescents.
Unlike other centrosaurines, Nasutoceratops had an accessory bone at the top center of the frill.
Nasutoceratops was an early-diverging member of Centrosaurinae.
Nasutoceratops and its closest relatives may have formed a distinct centrosaurine group called Nasutoceratopsini.
The purpose of the unusually deep front of the skull is unknown.
The deep front of the skull may have played a role in chewing.
The functions of ceratopsian frills and horns are debated.
Signalling has been proposed as a function of ceratopsian frills and horns.
Combat has been proposed as a function of ceratopsian frills and horns.
Species recognition has been proposed as a function of ceratopsian frills and horns.
The forward-pointing brow horns may have let Nasutoceratops lock horns with opponents, as modern bovids do.
The Kaiparowits Formation dates to the late Campanian.
The Kaiparowits Formation was deposited on the island continent of Laramidia.
The Western Interior Seaway divided North America down the middle at the time.
Wetlands dominated the Kaiparowits environment.
The Kaiparowits environment supported a diverse animal community.
Other ceratopsians lived in the Kaiparowits environment.
Researchers have proposed that Laramidia had separate dinosaur regions, each with its own native species.
The relationships between Nasutoceratops and other centrosaurines of roughly the same age partly informed the proposal of separate dinosaur regions.
The proposal that Laramidia had separate dinosaur regions has been contested.
Paleontological surveys of the Kaiparowits Formation at the monument have been conducted since 2000.
The Natural History Museum of Utah has conducted the surveys.
The Bureau of Land Management has conducted the surveys.

Preserving the area's fossils was one reason for establishing the monument.
Studying the area's fossils was one reason for establishing the monument.
The surveys yielded a wide range of unusual dinosaur fossils.
Field crews from other institutions also participated in the surveys.
The collaborative survey effort is called the Kaiparowits Basin Project.
The project uncovered three new ceratopsian taxa.

Lund was a technician at the time of the discovery.
